pulls.title: guix: map the whole DISTSRC in -fdebug-prefix-map
pulls.body:
Fixes #34414.

### Why

The Guix build scripts set `-fdebug-prefix-map=${DISTSRC}/src=.`. Generated sources (for example the capnp proxies) are in the build tree, outside `${DISTSRC}/src`, so their debug info kept the absolute `/distsrc-base/distsrc-<commit>-<host>/build/...` path. Sources from `src/` were relative. With two kinds of paths, it is hard to set up source path mapping in a debugger.

This maps `${DISTSRC}` instead, in `build_linux.sh`, `build_linux_gui.sh`, `build_win.sh` and `build_win_gui.sh`. The macOS scripts do not set `-fdebug-prefix-map`, so this PR does not change them.

### What changes in the debug paths

All source paths are now relative to the repository root:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Source in `src/` | `./netaddress.cpp` | `./src/netaddress.cpp` |
| Generated source | `/distsrc-base/distsrc-<commit>-<host>/build/src/ipc/capnp/init.capnp.proxy-client.c++` | `./build/src/ipc/capnp/init.capnp.proxy-client.c++` |

To find the sources in gdb, use the repository root as the source directory (`directory /path/to/bitcoin`) instead of `src/`.

### How I checked

- Guix build of this change on an x86_64 build machine, for the six Linux and Windows hosts.
- `readelf --debug-dump=info`, `--debug-dump=rawline` and `--debug-dump=str` of `libexec/bitcoin-node.dbg` (x86_64-linux-gnu): no `distsrc` string. Sources show as `./src/...`, generated capnp files as `./build/src/...`.
- `bitcoind.exe.dbg` from the Windows debug zip: no `distsrc` string.
- The only absolute paths left come from the Guix toolchain (glibc, libgcc). This change does not affect them.

I will post the Guix hashes for this commit in a comment. I do not have an aarch64 build machine at the moment, so a build from someone with one is welcome.

pulls.title: guix: compute --build triplet when lowering, not at load time
pulls.body:
### Why

`building-on` in `contrib/guix/toolchains.scm` reads `(%current-system)` once, when the module is loaded. `guix shell` loads the manifest before it applies `--system`, so the value is the system of the machine that runs the build, not the system that Guix builds for.

So a build with `ADDITIONAL_GUIX_ENVIRONMENT_FLAGS="--system=aarch64-linux"` on an x86_64 machine (for example with `qemu-binfmt-service-type`, to get an aarch64 build machine) configures the aarch64 cross toolchain with `--build=x86_64-guix-linux-gnu`. `gcc-cross-sans-libc` then fails to configure:

```
checking for CET support... configure: error: compiler and assembler with CET support are required for --enable-cet
```

### What changes

`building-on` becomes a procedure, and its three call sites call it. Guix then computes the triplet for each derivation, under the system that the derivation is built for.

### How I checked

- On master, `HOST=x86_64-linux-gnu guix shell -n --system=aarch64-linux -m contrib/guix/linux_static.scm` (with `toolchains.scm` on the load path, as `guix-build` does) gives `gcc-cross-sans-libc` with `--build=x86_64-guix-linux-gnu`. With this PR it gives `--build=aarch64-guix-linux-gnu`. That is the same derivation that `guix build -d --system=aarch64-linux` gives on master.
- Native builds (no `--system`): the toolchain derivations from `linux_static.scm` and `manifest_gui.scm` are identical on master and with this PR. So this PR does not change release builds.
- With this PR, an emulated aarch64 build of `x86_64-linux-gnu` on x86_64 built the whole cross toolchain and the non-GUI binaries. The GUI environment then failed in the tests of `python-pylint` (timeout under emulation) and `maturin` (snapshot mismatch). These packages have no aarch64 substitutes at the pinned Guix commit, and the failures are not related to this change.

pulls.title: init: reject -port=65535 when the onion port has to be derived from it
pulls.body:
The default onion bind uses -port + 1. With -port=65535 this wraps to 0, so the node binds 127.0.0.1 to a random port and the automatic onion service points there.

Now startup fails with a clear error when that port is needed. An explicit -bind=<addr>:<port>=onion still works, and so does -listen=0.

Added cases to feature_port.py.

pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: reject duplicate coins and empty snapshot groups
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Snapshot loading doesn't validate the announced coin count against the unique UTXOs loaded.
Repeated outpoints collapse into one coin, so a snapshot can repeat every record, announce the doubled count, and still match the committed UTXO hash.
`loadtxoutset` then reports the inflated count as `coins_loaded`.

Snapshot loading also accepts transaction groups with no coins.
They leave the UTXO hash unchanged and don't advance the coin count, so parsing them bypasses the interrupt check and can delay shutdown.

**Fix:** Compare the announced count with the unique coin count already produced by the existing UTXO statistics scan, and reject zero-count transaction groups while parsing the snapshot.
When both the content hash and coin count are wrong, loading reports the hash error first.

pulls.title: script: store interpreter stack elements as reference-counted objects
pulls.body:
Modifies the script interpreter to represent stack elements internally using smart pointers, making duplication memory-cheap, and giving us caching keys which are cheap and guaranteed unique by the compiler. First part of a 2-part project to improve script interpreter performance in preparation for PQ signatures. 

No consensus changes - a pure performance improvement refactor.

## Motivation 

We presently have `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520`, but in the near future, motivated by the need for PQ signature schemes, we may want to introduce soft fork changes which increase the max stack element size for new output types well into the multi-kilobyte range. This may be perhaps as high as 10kb or more given the current landscape of PQ signature schemes' sizes. 

Ongoing related work:

- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/main/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size
- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76

This poses a new problem to today's implementations if deployed naively. 

Today's Bitcoin script interpreter moves around raw mutable byte vectors to represent stack elements. When those elements are duplicated, the underlying byte vectors are deep-copied. When hash opcodes execute, they always invoke the corresponding hash function and fully ingest the top stack element. Duplication and hashing cost only a single weight unit in tapscript, with no upper limit on how many times they can be executed, aside from implicit limits due to the 10,000 byte script size maximum.

If we were to simply up the stack element size limit from 520b to 10kb, then we exacerbate an existing DoS vector on bitcoin nodes: Push a big (today 520b, maybe someday 10kb) stack element, then duplicate and hash it over and over. Worst case would be a script like this:

```cpp
<big_blob> DUP DUP [DUP3 RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP]...
```  

...with the `[...]` part repeating up to the script size limit. RMD160 is used because it lacks hardware acceleration support and so performs significantly worse than even HASH256 or HASH160, making a more effective CPU attack.

This costs the attacker only \~20000 weight units (10kb for the script, 10kb for the stack element), but forces all validators to evaluate OP_RIPEMD160 about 4284 times, each on the same 10kb input. That's about 672588 RMD160 compressions in software.

I ran a benchmark (not in this PR) using this style of script with 520b and 10kb script elements. 

- 520b: validation takes about **3 milliseconds**
- 10,000b: validation takes about **52 milliseconds**

## This PR

(idea credit: EthanHeilman)

To address this risk, we would want to implement a **hash cache** for all the hashing opcodes. However, to implement such a cache safely in consensus, we need extremely robust cache keys. A collision in the cache key would be a consensus bug because the cache would return the wrong hash for a given input. But we can't cryptographically hash the inputs to compute a cache key... that is the same work we are trying to avoid with the cache. 

Instead we can kill two birds with two PRs. 

1. Replace stack elements with ref-counting pointers, so OP_DUP et al duplicate pointers and not the underlying raw bytes. :arrow_backward:  **THIS PR**
2. Implement a hash cache keyed by the stack element pointers. Each cache entry holds a handle to the key pointer so that the key doesn't get dropped and the pointer reallocated for a new stack element (which would cause a consensus bug). Cache key uniqueness is guaranteed by the compiler.  :arrow_backward: **Future PR**

Stage 1 reduces the asymmetric memory inflation attack allowed by OP_DUP et al. Stage 2 fixes the asymmetric CPU DoS attack. To be clear, neither stage fully prevents an attacker from uploading a series of large stack elements, and duplicating/hashing them. But we **do** force attackers to pay for those operations with fees and block space. 

I have both stage 1 and 2 implemented locally and can show benchmarks to prove the effect of the cache, if desired. I could have submitted it all as one PR but both stages are atomic and could do well with separate review.

pulls.title: test: construct multisig_tests inputs/outputs declaratively
pulls.body:
Part of # 3 6 6 9 2. This replaces the field-by-field construction of transaction inputs and outputs in `multisig_tests` with `COutPoint`, `CTxIn` and `CTxOut` constructor calls.

It keeps `CMutableTransaction` as the builder, since a `CTransaction` constructor taking inputs and outputs directly is still under discussion (# 3 6 6 9 6). If one is added, the `vin`/`vout` lists here can be passed to it directly.

This change is test-only and does not change the constructed transactions:

- The funding outputs were previously created by `vout.resize(3)` and only had their `scriptPubKey` assigned, leaving `nValue` at its null value (`-1`). The `-1` is now spelled out explicitly, which makes this previously hidden value visible.
- The loop index is changed from `int` to `uint32_t` to match `COutPoint::n`, as brace-initialization does not allow the narrowing conversion.

To check that the transactions are identical, I temporarily built the old and new versions side by side in the same test run and compared them. Their txids and wtxids matched in both `multisig_verify` and `multisig_Sign`.

pulls.title: refactor: Use u64 consistently for flatfile sizes
pulls.body:
`unsigned` is a 32-bit integer (even on 64-bit platforms). File sizes are generally measured in 64-bit integers and using 32-bit integers or architecture-dependent integers is brittle and confusing.

So use u64 consistently for flatfile sizes in this refactor.

Also, use `LARGE_INTEGER`'s `QuadPart` on Windows, which is recommended since C++11.

Also, unit test VarInt overflow errors.

pulls.title: net: unify send pause state
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Each peer's send pause state is a flag plus a separate start timestamp.
Message queueing and socket sends each duplicate the transition logic that keeps the two in sync, and the inactivity check (which needs both), reads them separately.

**Fix:** Move the pause transitions into `CNode` accessors over one atomic timestamp.
The inactivity check then reads the pause status and start time as one snapshot.

Follow-up to #36667.

pulls.title: qa: check more socket API invariants for each platform we support
pulls.body:
This improves our `Sock` test coverage following CVE-2026-117350.

This leaves out the test for the specific case that led to the OOM until we [fix `select()` reporting](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36688#issue-6085527087) for urgent data, but i'm also trying not to fight the last battle too much. Instead i focused on trying to pin down all invariants Claude and I could come up with that could be reasonably tested. This will help us understand our code better, and get more assurance we do not break some assumption a (security critical) caller may be relying on further down the road.

Another goal is to tie the events our fuzzing mock can report to the events each OS actually reports, and when. A follow-up will extend the mock to match what these tests pin down. This wouldn’t have caught the CVE-2026-117350 bug: it was in the very logic the mock replaces, so a fuzz target could only have found it if the mock had been written with that bug in mind. But the next bug may well be somewhere else, and a mock that can report everything the real socket APIs can, lets the fuzzer reach corner cases which may lack a proper unit test.

A lot more coverage could be added. I chose not to add tests specific to the logic used for trusted interfaces (Tor control, the SOCKS5 proxy, I2P SAM) or to a single platform. I also left out the test which led me to find https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36688#issuecomment-6509375262, as this needs to be fixed first.

pulls.title: refactor: move block writes and pruning into BlockManager
pulls.body:
`FlushStateToDisk()` handles block storage directly. It applies `BlockManager`'s prune locks, writes its pruned flag, checks its blocks directory space and runs the flush, index write and file deletion, while `BlockManager` reads the chainstate to pick files. A pruning API on block storage (#35627) would have to go through validation for all of it.

This moves the storage side into `BlockManager`, as described in the same issue. Validation decides which heights may be pruned and passes them as limits. `BlockManager` applies its prune locks, selects the files, flushes, writes the index and deletes the files, in the same order as before. There is no behavior change to my knowledge.

Based on #36735

Thanks to musaHaruna for his [review on my fork](https://github.com/pzafonte/bitcoin/pull/2#pullrequestreview-5533305792), which led to grouping and checking the prune limits and to moving the prune bookkeeping into `BlockManager`.

pulls.title: fuzz: check GetStale() returns exactly the stale private broadcast txs
pulls.body:
The `private_broadcast` fuzz test checks each tx that `GetStale()` returns. This adds to it by checking that all stale txs are returned.  `ReattemptPrivateBroadcast()` only retries what `GetStale()` returns, and a stale tx left out is never retried.

This partly came up during review in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35129#pullrequestreview-4427536924, and recently also surfaced in https://mutanthub.space/mutants/3752 , where changing `continue` to `break` in `GetStale()` passes all current tests.

This PR records when each tx is added and when each node confirms it. Then it checks that `GetStale()` returns exactly the expected txs.

pulls.title: refactor: pass BlockManager to ChainstateManager
pulls.body:
`ChainstateManager` creates and owns its `BlockManager` which means block storage can't exist without chainstate management. Validation also reaches `BlockManager`'s members through friend declarations. In #35627, moving that ownership out of `ChainstateManager` which came up as worthwhile doing.

`ImportBlocks` gets `BlockManager::SetBlockfilesIndexed()` for the reindex flag and moves to node/chainstate, since it drives validation. `RequestPrune()` and `MarkBlockIndexDirty()` replace the friend declarations, keeping the prune check flag private. `NodeContext` and the kernel then create the `BlockManager` first, pass it to `ChainstateManager` by reference and destroy `ChainstateManager` first. Last, `ChainstateLoadOptions::prune` is removed, since every caller set it from the `BlockManager`'s prune mode.

The only behavior change to my knowledge is startup log order, because the block tree database opens before the script verification threads start.

Based on #36738

Thanks to musaHaruna for his [review on my fork](https://github.com/pzafonte/bitcoin/pull/2#pullrequestreview-5533305792), which suggested `RequestPrune()`.

pulls.title: test: SRD tie-break test
pulls.body:
Pr #33223  adjusts the weight selection to keep the lighter coin when two coins have the same value, but the test has two mistakes

1. It builds `mixed_weight_pool` but passes `utxo_pool` to `TestSRDSuccess`.
2. There is nothing enforcing coin eviction because the current max weight (`4 * 3 * 67` = 804 WU) fits any two coins (544 WU)

The old existing test does not check the fix:
If you reverse #33223, it still passes 20/20 tests, which means it misses the tie-break
Other coin selection tests like `spend_tests`, `wallet_send.py`, `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py` do not catch the broken tie-break
The fix
The PR uses `mixed_weight_pool` instead of `utxo_pool`.
The PR adds an extra light coin so that only two light coins can fit together and evicts a coin on every tie to pass.
It also lowers the max weight to `4 * 2 * (P2WPKH_INPUT_VSIZE - 1)` = 536 WU; SRD now has to evict the heavier coin on every tie to succeed
Adds a second (67 vB) light coin to the pool
This should show 20/20 failed tests with [bitcoin#33223](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33223) reverted and 20/20 passing without the revert
Steps to reproduce:
Revert the #33223  change in `src/wallet/coinselection.cpp`

```
git show eff9e798b9 -- src/wallet/coinselection.cpp | git apply -R
```

Build and run the tests

```
cmake --build build --target test_bitcoin
build/bin/test_bitcoin --run_test=coinselection_tests/srd_test
```

Expected results: After the revert, it should fail on this PR and pass on master

cc @yancyribbens

The Python shell linters, `lint-shell.py` and `lint-shell-locale.py`, now use `SHARED_EXCLUDED_SUBTREES` instead of maintaining hardcoded subtree exclusions.

pulls.title: rpc: Let dumptxoutset fail early on stale targets and concurrent runs
pulls.body:
This improves handling of two edge cases where `dumptxoutset` currently only fails after doing unnecessary and possibly incorrect work:

Stale rollback target (first commit): `ParseHashOrHeight` accepts any known block hash, and the rollback path never checks the target is on the active chain. The full UTXO set is copied and blocks are disconnected back from the tip only to fail when the target block height is reached. This is now rejected before all that as an invalid param, matching the check in `getchaintxstats` and `scanblocks`. This is a pretty unlikely scenario but the fix is also very small.

Concurrent calls (second commit): Nothing prevented triggering two runs at once and since this is a relatively long running operation I don't think it is that unlikely that this might happen by accident or that users think this might actually be a possible thing to do if you want two different dumps. On master currently both runs would write to `<path>.incomplete`, so the second dump to the same path corrupts the file the first one reports as successfully written. And also the prune lock has a fixed name, so the second run overwrites the first's height and the first to finish deletes the others lock mid-rollback. A second call now fails immediately with "dumptxoutset is already running". `TemporaryPruneLock` is extended and renamed to `DumptxoutsetGuard` and handles both the general running of multiple instances and the lock management. The alternative to this approach would be to allow for concurrent runs and fix that behavior but it seemed to me like that would be overengineering considering that the audience for this functionality should be very small.

pulls.title: coins: avoid redundant prevout preparation allocations
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Block preparation inserts an unused final transaction ID, repeatedly constructs salted transaction-ID sets, and allocates a worker-task vector. Small input queues also submit more tasks than can do useful work.

**Fix:** Insert each transaction ID before scanning the following transaction's inputs. Reuse the set's buckets and hash salt and the worker-task vector across blocks. Limit submitted tasks to the smaller of the worker and queued-input counts.

pulls.title: bugfix: send shortened IPv6 addresses to SOCKS5 proxies in full
pulls.body:
Found while auditing #36628 

Already known upstream issue with C-tor: https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/issues/32314

With `-proxy` pointed at Tor, outbound connections to IPv6 peers whose
 address contains an inner `::` always fail with "general failure".

 Core sends every SOCKS5 destination as a DOMAINNAME, with IPv6 in its
 compressed form. Tor copies the name into its relay BEGIN cell as
 `<name>:<port>`, and the exit's `tor_addr_port_split` first tries to parse
 the whole string as an IPv6 address. `2001:db8::1:8333` is a valid one,
 because the `::` absorbs the port as an eighth group. The exit then sees no
 port and closes the stream. Addresses written with all eight groups, or
 ending in `::`, are unaffected: appending `:port` to them does not give a
 valid address.

 About 20% of the IPv6 addresses in a gossip-filled addrman, and 29% of
 current IPv6 DNS seed answers, have an inner `::`. The failure is closed;
 there is no fallback to a direct connection.

 Note that this also effects private broadcast by default.

 This PR sends such addresses with all eight groups written out
 (`2001:db8:0:0:0:0:0:1`). `<name>:<port>` then has nine groups, so the exit
 splits at the last colon. Other forms:

 | Form                  | Tor         | Tor, SafeSocks 1 | getaddrinfo-based proxies |
 |-----------------------|-------------|------------------|---------------------------|
 | `2001:db8::1` (today) | fails       | fails            | works                     |
 | `[2001:db8::1]`       | works       | works            | fails                     |
 | ATYP IPv6             | works, logs a DNS-leak warning | refused | works         |
 | eight groups (this PR)| works       | works            | works                     |

 Tested against tor 0.4.9.13: on mainnet, master could not reach four
 seed-provided peers with inner-`::` addresses (30 "general failure"); with
 this change all four connected and completed the version handshake.
 `feature_proxy.py` and a new `netbase_tests` case check the bytes sent.

pulls.title: rpc: Manual prune lock management (Take 2)
pulls.body:
This is a refreshed version of #19463, which was closed due to inactivity.

Motivation: On pruned nodes, if a wallet is not loaded while the node is running, blocks necessary for rescanning when the wallet is loaded may be pruned. This PR allows users and external wallet software to manually manage prune locks via RPC, so they can protect blocks needed for future rescans and also clean up locks that are no longer relevant (e.g. after permanently unloading a wallet from a node). This is useful both for Bitcoin Core's own wallet and for external wallets that use Bitcoin Core as a backend. Usage of temporary prune locking may also be helpful in other functional test scenarios but I didn't spend time to check where might apply.

This PR leverages the existing prune locks system we already have. The interface of the RPCs of the old PR has been slightly updated, it now matches the pattern used by `setban`/`listbanned` exactly. The locks are prefixed to distinguish them from the systems locks and prevent naming colissions. They are not persisted across restarts.

pulls.title: CAT in Tapscript (BIP-347)
pulls.body:
# CAT in Tapscript

This PR provides the necessary code to enable the opcode OP\_CAT in Tapscript as specified in [BIP-347: OP\_CAT in Tapscript](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0347.mediawiki) and [BIN-2024-0001](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/binana/blob/master/2024/BIN-2024-0001.md),

**Important:** This PR *does not* include miner activation functionality. This means that merging this PR into bitcoin-core will not make OP\_CAT functional in Bitcoin.
If this PR is merged it is *not* a signal of community consensus around activating CAT nor be read as a portent about the activation process or timeline.
The PR is not a stand-in for consensus around such decisions.

This PR includes:

- An implementation of the Tapscript opcode OP\_CAT along with the flags `SCRIPT_VERIFY_OP_CAT` and `SCRIPT_VERIFY_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT`.
- Integration and unit tests which ensure that our CAT  implementation works as expected. This includes ensuring that CAT never uses more that 520 bytes of stack memory. A full description of what these tests cover is given below.
- An improvement to `src/test/script_tests.cpp` JSON script format enabling the rapid creation of new Tapscript unit tests.

## Activation on Bitcoin-inquisition (signet)

[Bitcoin-inquisition PR 37](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/39) which contained our implementation of OP\_CAT [was merged into bitcoin-inquisition (signet) on Apr 25 2024](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/39), released as [bitcoin-inquisition release 25.2 on Apr 26 2024.](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/releases/tag/v25.2-inq) and activated in bitcoin-inquisition Apr 30 2024. The bitcoin-inquisition PR was reviewed in the PR review club [(transcript of discussion)](https://bitcoincore.reviews/bitcoin-inquisition-39). Since Apr 30 2024 there have been many OP\_CAT transactions created and spent on signet.

The code merged into bitcoin-inquisition differs from this PR, as we have removed the consensus logic which was used to activate it on signet.

## OP\_CAT Tapscript Implementation

We implement OP\_CAT as a new Tapscript op code by redefining the opcode OP\_SUCCESS126 (126 in decimal and 0x7e in hexadecimal). This is the same opcode value used by the original OP_CAT.

When evaluated, the OP\_CAT instruction:

1. Pops the top two values off the stack,
2. concatenates the popped values together in stack order,
3. and then pushes the concatenated value on the top of the stack.

OP\_CAT fails if there are fewer than two values on the stack or if a concatenated value would have a combined size greater than the maximum script element size of 520 bytes.

See [BIP 347](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0347.mediawiki) for a deeper description.

### Errors thrown

If evaluated OP\_CAT can throw the following errors:

- If at time of evaluation the stack has fewer than two elements we throw the error: `SCRIPT_ERR_INVALID_STACK_OPERATION`
- If at time of evaluation the top two stack elements have a combined size greater than `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE` (520 bytes) we throw the error: `SCRIPT_ERR_PUSH_SIZE`.

### Script verification flags

While this PR does not contain any miner signaling and activation logic and can not activate OP\_CAT, it does contain two flags which future activation logic could set to control activation of OP\_CAT.

- `SCRIPT_VERIFY_OP_CAT` IF a bitcoin node has this set to true, then it treat OP\_CAT enabled for Tapscript. That is, OP\_SUCCESS126 will be redefining to OP\_CAT in Tapscript. If this was set to true at the consensus level this would cause a soft fork.

`SCRIPT_VERIFY_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` When set to true, a node receiving any Tapscript transaction containing the opcode OP\_CAT or OP\_SUCCESS126 will reject the transaction throwing the error `SCRIPT_ERR_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` but not banning the node which relayed the transaction. This prevents nodes from relaying transactions with OP\_CAT. This  is equivalent to the behavior of `SCRIPT_ERR_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT = true` when `SCRIPT_VERIFY_OP_CAT = false` as OP\_CAT is an OP\_SUCCESS (OP\_SUCCESS126).

This is how these two flags are intended to be used to ensure a smooth soft fork.

| Stage | `SCRIPT_VERIFY OP_CAT` | `SCRIPT_VERIFY DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1.Default** | False | True | This does not represent any change in behavior of the bitcoin-core node. |
| **2.Upgrading** | True | True | OP\_CAT is activating. |
| **3.Upgraded** | True | False | It is clear that OP\_CAT has been activated and the network has been upgraded. |

The flag `SCRIPT_ERR_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` provides a window of time for the network to fully activate, before nodes will relay or accept transactions containing OP\_CAT in their mem pools.

## Tests

This PR contains a suite of script tests to ensure that OP\_CAT functions as expected. In the JSON script tests (`script_tests.json`), we test:

- That if OP\_CAT is not activated that there are no changes to bitcoin consensus.
- That regardless of the activation or non-activation of OP\_CAT in Tapscript, pre-Tapscript scripts, i.e. Bitcoin scripts, have no changes in behavior.
- That OP\_CAT when evaluated throws the expected error when there are less than two elements on the stack.
- That OP\_CAT when evaluated in a variety of circumstances and edge cases, successfully concatenates elements of the stack. This includes:
  - multiple calls to OP\_CAT in a row,
  - evaluating OP\_CAT inside of a IF conditional,
  - evaluating OP\_CAT on zero size stack elements, random and large stack elements,
  - evaluating OP\_CAT on values being moved to and from the alt stack,
  - and checking that when evaluated OP\_CAT concatenates the elements in the expected order.

All of these tests are designed to cover the happy path of OP\_CAT, the various errors which OP\_CAT can throw and all the corner cases between those two outcomes.

Additionally we include three tests outside of the JSON script tests.

- `cat_simple` and `cat_empty_stack` are designed to test OP\_CAT outside of the JSON serialization regime. Ensure that we catch bugs that we might miss in the JSON script tests due to a bug introduced at the JSON serialization layer.
- `cat_dup_test` enumerates all stack element sizes from 1 to 522 bytes and then enumerates up to 10 repetitions of `OP\_DUP OP\_CAT`. It then tests if the stack element would exceed 520 bytes and if so did OP\_CAT throw the error `SCRIPT_ERR_PUSH_SIZE`. This allows us to be certain that OP\_CAT will not introduce any `OP\_DUP OP\_CAT` memory exhaustion attacks.

### Better Tapscript tests in JSON script tests

While writing these JSON script tests (`script_tests.json`) we ran into the following problem. The JSON script tests are simple and easy to write for pre-Tapscript scripts, but adding or changing a Tapscript test requires substantial work per test.
Consider the following pre-tapscript test:

```json
["'aa' 'bb'", "CAT 0x4c 0x02 0xaabb EQUAL", "P2SH,STRICTENC", "DISABLED_OPCODE", "CAT disabled"]
```

whereas a Tapscript test for the same script (annotated with comments for better readability) would look like:

```json
[
    [
        "aa",
        "bb",
        "7e4c02aabb87", // output script
        "c0d6889cb081036e0faefa3a35157ad71086b123b2b144b649798b494c300a961d", // control block
        0.00000001
    ],
    "",
    "0x51 0x20 0x15048ed3a65748549c27b671936987093cf73a4c9cb18522a74fb9553060ca99", // Tapscript output
    "P2SH,WITNESS,TAPROOT",
    "OK",
    "TAPSCRIPT CATs aa and bb together and checks if EQUAL to aabb"
]
```

Computing the Tapscript output, such as `0x51 0x20 0x15048ed3a65748549c27b671936987093cf73a4c9cb18522a74fb9553060ca99`, requires writing custom code and running it for each test. The same is true for the Tapscript control block, such as `c0d6889cb081036e0faefa3a35157ad71086b123b2b144b649798b494c300a961d`. If a test is changed or updated new outputs and control blocks must be computed. The complexity of doing this is likely the reason that no one has added any Tapscript tests to JSON script tests until this PR.

In this PR we address this issue by adding the following improvements to JSON script tests:

- Adding simple macros (`"#SCRIPT#` and `#CONTROLBLOCK#`) that allow the script test parser to automatically generate and inject a valid Tapscript output and control block to be computed automatically from the JSON script.
- Allowing Tapscript scripts to use the human readable strings like pre-script scripts by marking the location of the script in the witness stack using `#SCRIPT#`. This transforms the unreadable script `7e4c02aabb87` into `#SCRIPT# CAT 0x4c 0x02 0xaabb EQUAL`.

This results in the following JSON script test which is far easier to write and easier to read.

```json
[
    [
        "aa",
        "bb",
        "#SCRIPT# CAT",
        "#CONTROLBLOCK#",
        0.00000001
    ],
    "",
    "0x51 0x20 #TAPROOTOUTPUT#",
    "P2SH,WITNESS,TAPROOT,OP_CAT",
    "OK",
    "TAPSCRIPT Test of OP_CAT flag by calling CAT on two elements. TAPSCRIPT_OP_CAT flag is set so CAT is executed."
],
```

pulls.title: ipc: Expose Chain interface to IPC clients
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Processes connected to `bitcoin-node` over IPC (with `-ipcbind`) can use the `Mining` interface, but they can't currently use the `Chain` interface read chain data or follow chain events. Chain data could be useful to third-party clients and Bitcoin Core's own wallet could use this as well to run in a separate process (#10102). But exposing all of `interfaces::Chain` to external clients would make its methods hard to change, since the wallet uses them as internal API (#34981).

**Solution:** Add capnp wrappers for `interfaces::Chain`, split into two interfaces backed by the same C++ class:

- `Chain`, returned by `Init.makeChain`, is stable. It follows Cap'n Proto schema evolution rules, so existing clients keep working as methods are added. It starts with the five block lookup methods: `findBlock`, `findFirstBlockWithTimeAndHeight`, `findAncestorByHeight`, `findAncestorByHash` and `findCommonAncestor`.
- `UnstableChain`, returned by `Init.makeUnstableChain`, extends `Chain` with every other method, for Bitcoin Core's own clients. It can change in any way between releases. Incompatible changes renumber `makeUnstableChain`, so old clients get an error instead of calling the wrong methods.

Methods can move from `UnstableChain` to `Chain` once we're willing to support them for external use. `test/functional/interface_ipc.py` shows a Python client calling both interfaces. Like the existing IPC interfaces, these are only available to processes that can connect to the IPC socket, which already grants full node access through `Init.makeRpc`.

**Merge order:** This depends on bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#377 and bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#379 and a subtree update that includes them (this PR currently carries that bump, plus a `-Wc++23-lambda-attributes` build fix that goes with it), and on #36520, which fixes node crashes IPC clients could trigger with invalid `Chain` arguments.

refactor: Use CBlockIndex parameters as reference
pulls.body:
This is a janitorial refactor, a continuation of #34440. Input method parameters of type `const CBlockIndex*` are changed to reference `const CBlockIndex&` in some places where it makes no sense to call with a nullptr.

Motivation: slight improvement in code quality, maintainability and robustness.
- more explicit representation of the non-null input invariant
- less chance of nullptr-access error with future code changes
- more explicit checks at call sites for the non-null input invariant.

The following methods are affected:
- `LastCommonAncestor()` in chain.h
- `PeerManagerImpl::FindNextBlocks()` (net_processing.cpp)
- `PeerManagerImpl::TryDownloadingHistoricalBlocks()` (net_processing.cpp)
- `BlockFilterIndex::LookupFilterRange()`, `BlockFilterIndex::LookupFilterHashRange()` (blockfilterindex.h), and `LookupRange()` in blockfilterindex.cpp
- `BaseIndex::ProcessBlock()` (base.h)

General guidelines:
- When a method has an input of type `const CBlockIndex*`, and by contract it cannot be nullptr, change it to `const CBlockIndex&`. The reference type is an implicit documentation of the nun-nullptr invariant.
- When calling a method with reference parameter, ensure that it cannot be nullptr (it is often derived from a pointer), by/because:
  - explicit prior check and error handling
  - an assert/Assert/Assume
  - itself being a non-nullptr invariant input
  - it is being an output from a method with no-nullptr output invariant
- For local variables, use reference types whenever possible, for non-nullptr references
- For technical reasons pointers are still used even in some non-nullptr cases:
  - containers/variables that can staty unitialized initially
  - containers that need `reserve()`
  - using reference type in `std::set` would result in some copy constructor calls
  - `std::optional` cannot hold a reference type

pulls.title: rpc: reset id and version per batch element
pulls.body:
In a JSON-RPC batch, an element that is not an object gets an error reply with the id and version of the element before it.

`ExecuteHTTPRPC` uses one request object for the whole batch. `parse()` throws on a non-object before it resets `id` and `m_json_version`. For `[{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"getblockcount","id":"X"}, 2]` the reply has two objects with `"id":"X"`, one with a result and one with an error. If the first element is a notification, the error is dropped. I reset both fields at the top of `parse()`, so the error is the one the first element of a batch already gets. The new case in `interface_rpc.py` fails on master and passes with this change.

pulls.title: net: option to disallow v1 connection on ipv4 and ipv6 peers
pulls.body:
resolves #29618.

This PR adds a config flag option `-v2onlyclearnet` which disallows outbound v1 connections on ipv4 and ipv6 networks since they're unencrypted. outbound v1 connections are still possible from tor/i2p/cjdns peers since they're encrypted networks.

- v1 outbound connections to peers are not attempted
- v1 reconnections are not attempted (if peer is falsely advertised as v2 peer and we attempt a v2 connection but it fails, we do not attempt a v1 reconnection when `-v2onlyclearnet` is switched on)

Currently 70% of reachable nodes in network supporting v2 (according to https://21.ninja/reachable-nodes/node-service-share/ and https://bitnodes.io/nodes). Also found 81% of addresses supporting v2 in the addrman of nodes I checked - personal node and the nodes in [peer.observer](https://peer.observer/addrman/alice). (You can use [this branch ](https://github.com/stratospher/bitcoin/commits/addrinfo_service_display/)to check the % of v2 addresses in a node's addrman.)

EDIT: see [summary](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30951#issuecomment-4346061700) on pros and cons for whether to allow v2 inbounds or not for `-v2onlyclearnet`.

pulls.title: validation: improve block data I/O error handling in P2P paths
pulls.body:
Early note: the majority of this PR consists of test coverage. The changes per se are quite small, just the issue shows up in multiple paths in slightly different forms.

The goal of the PR is to ensure I/O errors are not silently ignored during validation or P2P message handling. In some cases, such as `GETDATA` or `GETBLOCKTXN` requests, errors can be swallowed, leaving the node unresponsive to the request without any action. In a harder to reach but more severe case, a swallowed error can leave the node alive but stuck, unable to process new blocks and advance the chain. Also, silently ignoring errors obviously makes problems harder to diagnose. So this PR seeks to improve all of that.

Currently, the same root cause, inability to access the blocks directory, can produce different behaviors depending on where it occurs: 
1. If it happens during block connection, inside `AcceptBlock()`, the error gets caught and triggers a fatal error graceful shutdown. This is the correct behavior.

2. If it happens during block connection (due to the unguarded `FlatFileSeq::Open` -> `fs::create_directories` call), after `AcceptBlock()`, inside `ActivateBestChain()`, the error gets thrown and swallowed by the P2P general try-catch, leaving the node in a living but stuck state. Where `ActivateBestChain()` will always silently fail on any posterior block processing, retrying to active the failing block.

3. If it happens during `GETDATA` request, the file system error gets swallowed by the message handling general try-catch, only logging a net-debug-level message. The remote peer is not disconnected, nor the node aborts. It just silently ignores the request. This is different to a missing block data, which currently logs the error + disconnects the peer.

4. If it happens during `GETBLOCKTXN` request, the file system error either gets swallowed by the message handling general try-catch or crashes the system via an assertion, depending on if the problem is at the blocks directory level or at the block data level, which is inconsistent.

5. If it happens during `GETCFILTERS` request, the file system error gets swallowed by the message handling general try-catch.

6. If this happens in any of the index functions, the node crashes.


So, this PR makes failure handling consistent and ensures the node never enters a stuck state due to a block I/O error. Changes:

1. `GETDATA` now treats the issue in the same way as other I/O errors: it logs the error + disconnect the remote peer.
2. `GETBLOCKTXN` now triggers a fatal error and graceful shutdown. The error here is stricter than in `GETDATA` because it can only access the last 10 blocks, which must be available for reorgs.
3. `ActivateBestChain()` now triggers a fatal error and graceful shutdown when it happens. Fixing the silent stuck node state scenario.
4. `GETCFILTERS` now logs the error through the expected path: "Failed to find block filter in index". A more descriptive error message can be added in a follow-up PR.
5. The index-related functions now ignore the error instead of crashing the node. This matches how the code was written, as these paths were not expecting `OpenFile` to throw. Better error handling can be added in a follow-up PR.


Testing Note
Can reproduce the different behaviors that cause the stuck node scenario by running the second commit’s unit test 28af683b5dfdce88892e367b308857b94ec630fe or by manually introducing an exception in `ConnectTip()` (which occurs inside `ActivateBestChain()`). Previously, the thrown exception would have being caught by the general P2P try-catch and logged only at net-debug level, which most users do not have enabled, leaving the node alive but stuck, as subsequent block connections repeatedly attempt to process the failing block, throw the exception again, and get silently swallowed. Adding a functional test for this scenario is not possible due to the requirement of failing inside `ActivateBestChain()`, which always occurs after `AcceptBlock()`, which correctly captures the error.


Separate Note
There is another assertion scenario that we can move to graceful shutdown (fatal error) in the compact block relay that I haven't done here.

Extra Note
If want to see a similar error producing a crash, but in the wallet, go to #34176.

pulls.title: txindex: allow running in pruned mode
pulls.body:
After #35531, each txindex entry now points to the block hash containing the tx instead of the file location of the block. The block hash is then used to find the file position of the block to read the tx from. This allows us to determine the hash of the containing block even if the block is later pruned, and also determine the location of the block on disk if it is later downloaded again via `getblockfrompeer`.

This PR enables maintaining a txindex while pruned. If a txid lookup tries to read a tx from a pruned block, the hash of the missing block is surfaced to the caller.

If desired, a user may call `getblockfrompeer` using the returned hash to download the block, then try again successfully. The downloaded block will be added to the front of the block queue, so won't be pruned again for at least 288 blocks. Of course a larger prune setting is desired if lots of historical blocks will be read, and there are privacy issues if the user is looking up their own transactions. Ideally the blocks can be fetched from a trusted node or from random peers with decoy blocks fetched occasionally.

Resolves https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/10609, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/12651, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/16182, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35240

pulls.title: wallet: start descriptor top up at range_start instead of index 0
pulls.body:
DescriptorScriptPubKeyMan::TopUpWithDB() expands the descriptor from m_max_cached_index + 1, which is 0 for a freshly imported descriptor regardless of its range_start. Importing a descriptor with "range": [N, M] therefore derives and watches every index in [0, M), so the cost of an import is O(M) rather than O(M - N) and the wallet treats scriptPubKeys below N as its own. Load() only expands [range_start, range_end), so those scriptPubKeys stop being IsMine the next time the wallet is opened, and a transaction picked up for one of them during the import rescan is no longer credited to the wallet.

Since ParseDescriptorRange() only bounds the size of the range and not its start, "range": [2146483648, 2147483647] is accepted and expands 2^31 indexes into m_map_script_pub_keys before the RPC returns.

Start the top up loop at range_start and record the index that was actually cached instead of counting from -1, so that Load() and TopUpWithDB() agree on m_max_cached_index for descriptors with a non-zero range_start. Before this change Load() left m_max_cached_index at range_end - range_start - 1 for such descriptors, which made the first top up after opening the wallet re-expand the stored range.

Importing wpkh(xpub/0/*) with "range": [600000, 600009] into a blank watch-only wallet goes from 19.5s to 0.09s on this machine.

pulls.title: compressor: oversized script decoding can leave a spendable script
pulls.body:
**Problem:** The oversized-script fallback appends `OP_RETURN` to the destination instead of replacing it. If the destination already contains an unfinished push, the appended byte becomes pushed data and the result can remain spendable.

**Fix:** Replace the destination with `OP_RETURN` rather than appending it.

Found while reviewing #36280. This predates that PR and appears latent because oversized outputs are excluded from the UTXO set, but it could affect malformed stored records decoded into a reused destination.

pulls.title: cli: Parse -signetchallenge like bitcoind
pulls.body:
`bitcoind` returns an useful error when invalid hex is passed to `-signetchallenge`:

```
$ bitcoind -signet -signetchallenge=z
Error: -signetchallenge must be hex, not 'z'
```

The error returned by `bitcoin-cli` only indicates that the RPC cookie wasn't found. It doesn't hint at invalid hex:

```
$ bitcoin-cli -signet -signetchallenge=z getblockcount
error: Authorization failed: ...
Is your -signetchallenge correct for custom signets?
```

To have consistent validation of signet args in `bitcoind` and `bitcoin-cli`, we now parse `-signetchallenge` in a new `ReadSignetChallengeArg()` function which is called in `GetSignetDataDir()` and `ReadSigNetArgs()`.

Addresses https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34566#discussion_r3668123074

I didn't add a release note because I don't think this change of an error message warrants one.

pulls.title: fuzz: add a custom mutator for PSBT
pulls.body:
The `partially_signed_transaction_deserialize` target feeds raw bytes to the PSBT parser. Byte-level mutations rarely produce well-formed key-value maps with valid keydata (pubkeys, xpubs, control blocks, DER signatures, etc), so most inputs are rejected early and the deeper per-field parsing is rarely reached.

This PR adds a custom mutator for PSBT which is ported from bitcoinfuzz (with some changes).  The mutator splits the input into global/input/output maps of key-value records, applies the mutations and serializes the result again. The first commit is a preparation to allow targets to provide a custom mutator by adding an optional `mutator` field to
`FuzzTargetOptions`. 

note: LLM assisted on porting the custom mutator.

pulls.title: psbt: verify final scripts in FinalizePSBT
pulls.body:
`finalizepsbt` can return `complete: true` and a hex for a PSBT whose `PSBT_IN_FINAL_SCRIPTWITNESS` (or final scriptSig) is invalid.

`FinalizePSBT` counts an input as complete when `SignPSBTInput` succeeds. If the input already has final fields, `PSBTInput::FillSignatureData` marks the sigdata complete and `ProduceSignature` returns true early (sign.cpp:752), before the script is verified. So the existing final fields are trusted as-is.

To reproduce, take a signed P2WPKH v0 PSBT that has a `non_witness_utxo` and flip one bit of the signature inside the final witness:
- `finalizepsbt` returns `complete: true` and a hex
- `analyzepsbt` says the input is not final, `next: finalizer`
- `testmempoolaccept` on the hex fails with `mempool-script-verify-flag-failed (Signature must be zero for failed CHECK(MULTI)SIG operation)`

Inputs that only have a `witness_utxo` already come out incomplete because of the `require_witness_sig` check, so this affects inputs with a `non_witness_utxo`.

#30357 fixed the same problem in `FillPSBT` by checking `PSBTInputSignedAndVerified`, and #33014 did it for `descriptorprocesspsbt`. This does the same in `FinalizePSBT`. Taproot verification needs every spent output. If one is missing, that input already fails in `SignPSBTInput` with `MISSING_INPUTS` and makes the PSBT incomplete, so the extra check doesn't change the result in that case.

The new test in `rpc_psbt.py` builds that PSBT and checks that `finalizepsbt` returns `complete: false` with no hex. It fails on master and passes with the fix. `wallet_musig.py` and the `psbt_wallet_tests` / `script_tests` unit tests still pass.

One behaviour change: a final script that is valid by consensus but non-standard now gives `complete: false`. `FillPSBT` and `descriptorprocesspsbt` already behave that way, since they check with the same standard flags.

pulls.title: rpc: Properly throw on internal I/O errors in GetTransaction
pulls.body:
Currently the GetTransaction return value is a nullable transaction
pointer, where nullptr represents two different outcomes: I/O error and
missing tx.

Reporting a confirmed transaction as missing is wrong, so properly
return an error instead.

pulls.title: btcsignals: destroy callbacks on disconnect
pulls.body:
Currently callback functions connected to signals do not get freed when their `connection::disconnect` method is called or when their associated `scoped_connection` is destroyed. They live as long as the signal does, even if they will never be called, and can only get [garbage collected](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/0fd515bbb7070a502dd2fe6d16f5f3cbac591283/src/util/btcsignals.h#L240-L241) if new connections are added.

This behavior is different that previous boost signals behavior and causes a [deadlock](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/actions/runs/31848571315/job/94919834743) on GUI shutdown in #10102 because when the node registers signal callbacks (`handleInitMessage`, etc) that get forwarded to the GUI, the callbacks own `mp::EventLoopRef` references, and if the callbacks aren't freed, the node process can't shut down.

This change restores boost signals behavior freeing callbacks when they are disconnected or when `scoped_connection` objects are destroyed to avoid this problem and make callback lifetimes more predictable.

pulls.title: rpc: generateblock to allow multiple outputs
pulls.body:
## Generatetomany

First approach was to create a `generatetomany` rpc call. That approach can be seen here https://github.com/polespinasa/bitcoin/pull/3

## Generateblock
Modifies `generateblock` to allow a user to set multiple outputs in the coinbase transaction. If an empty set is provided, the block will be empty. If no set of transactions is provided, the block will mine the mempool. If a set of transactions is provided only that set of txs will be mined.

```
$./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock bcrt1qw6qkj8wtw5hraxwxjp08m4aymkntms3yhqyacj
{
  "hash": "7359a3ed7af0f18f4016e6cb29193bd787a2452c584781135c585d5204b9ec5b"
}

$ ./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock '["bcrt1qal6p633hvwz2yp5mav0qy7u2az8gkn2xywnj6v", "bcrt1qvr3qgyhw6y0e0zj97v0j5yc40xtpea4wqj0g43"]'
{
  "hash": "6db028454b26d6667dd6df45be2772844121fb44f86433f6bbfbafa429974684"
}

$ ./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock '["bcrt1qal6p633hvwz2yp5mav0qy7u2az8gkn2xywnj6v", "bcrt1qvr3qgyhw6y0e0zj97v0j5yc40xtpea4wqj0g43"]' []

{
  "hash": "33e2ddc52546ddb0edf28bef5b295ee8fbd487b8aca19c97018467e2477877df"
}

```

### Motivation
https://x.com/SuperTestnet/status/1921220086645342550

Citating @supertestnet 
> When mining a block on regtest, the command "generatetoaddress" is available if you want to send the entire coinbase to 1 address. Let's add generatetomany in case you want to split up the coinbase among multiple addresses, similar to how the "sendtoaddress" and "sendmany" commands both exist and let you send money to (1) one address or (2) multiple addresses. The generatetomany command would be particularly useful for simulating protocols that send money to multiple recipients directly from a coinbase, as several pools do now, like ocean and braidpool.

pulls.title: consensus: Remove special treatment for single threaded script checking
pulls.body:
This topic has been motivated by my work on batch validation and a related conversation just happened here: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32467#discussion_r2098305199 

`CheckInputScripts` currently only does what its name implies if there is no multithreading usage for validation. If there are worker threads available the function instead only creates the checks and puts them into a vector. Aside from some shared pre-checks the multithreaded code path is much simpler compared to the rest. This dual use makes the function hard to grasp and its naming confusing.

This PR refactors this code to be more readable and improves documentation aside from unifying the single threaded and the multithreaded cases by letting checkqueue handle single threaded script checking as well. The code is already suited for this and there seems to be not noticable performance overhead from this.

pulls.title: wallet: allow skipping script paths
pulls.body:
While testing MuSig2 integration in #29675 I ran into a Ledger bug https://github.com/LedgerHQ/app-bitcoin-new/issues/329 that was triggered because we signed for a script path in addition to the key path. The bug itself will be fixed, but it seems useful in general to be able to skip script path signing (and finalizing).

For example, you may have a 2-of-2 musig() descriptor with some sort of fallback after coins are N blocks old. For both on chain privacy and fee reasons, you don't want to use this path unless absolutely necessary. But our wallet can't know if our co-signer still has their key, so we sign the script path at all times. This could lead to accidental broadcast.

This PR introduces a `keypath_only` option (default `false` for now) to the following RPC methods:
- `send` 
- `sendall`
- `walletcreatefundedpsbt`
- `walletprocesspsbt`
- `descriptorprocesspsbt`

The resulting PSBT won't _add_ `taproot_scripts` or `taproot_script_path_sigs`. It does still have `taproot_bip32_derivs` and `musig2_participant_pubkeys`.

It will not remove `taproot_scripts` from an existing PSBT, but it won't add a corresponding entry to `taproot_script_path_sigs`. We also won't finalize a PSBT without keypath spend, even with complete script paths. This protects against other participants accidentally including them.

The `wallet_taproot.py` tests are expanded to cover this behavior.

It can also be tested with https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/pull/91.

pulls.title: addrman, rpc: classify linked-IPv4 addresses consistently
pulls.body:
Some addresses can be an IPv6 ones with an embedded IPv4 address belongs to. `AddrMan::Size()`, and so the per-network counts in `getaddrmaninfo`, use `GetNetwork()`, which returns ipv6 for these addresses. However, the network filter in `GetAddr_()` and the network / source_network labels in `getnodeaddresses` and `getrawaddrman` use `GetNetClass()`, which returns ipv4 for them.

So on master, for example, for a node whose addrman holds a 6to4 or Teredo address:
  - getaddrmaninfo counts it under ipv6.
  - getnodeaddresses 0 "ipv6" doesn't return it.
  - getnodeaddresses 0 "ipv4" does return it, labelled ipv4.

This PR changes all of this places to use `GetNetwork()`. This way the filter, labels and the counts agree. We should leave `GetNetClass()` usage for netgroup and bucketing decisions, where treating linked-IPv4 addresses as IPv4 is intended. If you pick the change in the fuzz target and run it without the other changes, it's expected to crash to reproduce the issue.

pulls.title: Indexes: Harden the flush-error notification invariant
pulls.body:
This is a follow-up to #35714 as it has the two commits of that PR, do not merge or review before that PR

#35714 makes `FlushStateToDisk()` return `state.Error(...)` when `FlushChainstateBlockFile()` fails, relying on the comment `// FlushChainstateBlockFile() already emitted the flush-error notification.`

That invariant holds today, but it is not guaranteed by construction: it depends on every `success = false` branch inside `FlushBlockFile`/`FlushUndoFile` emitting the notification on its own. A future flush source (a new file type, a new error branch) that sets `success = false` **without** notifying would make `FlushStateToDisk()` return an error without `AbortNode()`.

This PR makes sure that **whenever a flush reports failure, the flush-error notification has been emitted**:

- **test: cover FlushBlockFile flush-error notifications**: lower-level `BlockManager` tests (as suggested in the #35714 review) that inject a failure on the block file and on the undo file separately and assert each failure emits `flushError`.
- **blockstorage: encapsulate flush+notify in FlushFile**:  a single `FlushFile()` helper couples the flush and the notification; `FlushBlockFile`/`FlushUndoFile` delegate to it. Behaviour is unchanged.

private broadcast: wait synchronously for mempool acceptance
pulls.body:
Calling `BroadcastTransaction` with the `NO_MEMPOOL_PRIVATE_BROADCAST` method skips inserting the transaction into the mempool and returns immediately. This causes problems with software that expects the transaction to be in the mempool after the function returns. For example many third-party wallets or services call `sendrawtransaction` and expect the transaction to be in the mempool after it returns a successful response.

This PR adds a new `TransactionAddedToMempoolSync` method to `CValidationInterface`. This is then used in `BroadcastTransaction` when the method is `NO_MEMPOOL_PRIVATE_BROADCAST` to wait for the transaction to have been accepted back into the mempool before returning. It also adds a timeout (default 10 minutes) to `BroadcastTransaction` and exposes it as an option for `sendrawtransaction`. Setting the timeout to 0 disables the wait and returns immediately, preserving the current behavior.

Synchronously waiting for mempool acceptance is also a prerequisite for adding private broadcast support to the wallet. The `TransactionAddedToMempoolSync` method is added specifically for future wallet broadcasting, so a broadcast caller holding `cs_wallet` will not timeout waiting on another background event that is also trying to acquire `cs_wallet`.

pulls.title: wallet: return broadcast errors from CommitTransaction
pulls.body:
Part of https://github.com/bitcoin-core/gui-qml/issues/1008.

The QML GUI shows "Transaction sent" even when the node rejected the transaction, because `CWallet::CommitTransaction()` only logs the rejection and returns `void`. 
This PR bubbles up the submission result through `interfaces::Wallet::commitTransaction()` so the GUI can report it.

#### Key changes
- Introduce `TransactionBroadcastError`, holding a `TransactionError` code and an untranslated message.
- Commit/Broadcast functions returns `Expected<void, TransactionBroadcastError>`. 
  - Remove `TransactionError::OK`, a success value in an error enum.
- Add a `SUBMISSION_SKIPPED` code for when the wallet doesn't submit the transaction (broadcasting disabled, abandoned, coinbase, confirmed or conflicted). `SubmitTxMemoryPoolAndRelay()` previously returned `false` in these cases.

#### Note
- Existing callers (wallet RPCs, Qt widgets, fee bumper) ignore the new result, so their behavior and RPC responses don't change.
- `commitBumpTransaction()` similarly reports success for a rejected replacement. This will be addressed in a follow-up PR.
- gui-qml will need to update its `interfaces::Wallet` mock for the new `commitTransaction()` signature.

pulls.title: wallet: relax external_signer flag constraints
pulls.body:
The `external_signer` indicates that an external signer device may be called via [HWI](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/HWI) or [equivalent](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/external-signer.md#signer-api) application.

When it was initially introduced some additional constraints were placed on wallets with this flag: it had to be a descriptor wallet and watch-only. Also the flag could not be added or removed later.

The constraints aren't a problem for the main supported and documented use case of connecting a single hardware wallet and using it just like a normal single sig Bitcoin Core wallet.

But they get in the way of MuSig2 support, see https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/pull/91.

This pull request drops the following constraints:

- `disable_private_keys` is no longer mandatory (but still default)
- `external_signer` flag is now mutable

Changing the `external_signer` flag reloads the wallet so that its descriptor ScriptPubKeyMans are recreated using the new setting.

Additionally it does the following:

- make the `blank` option for `createwallet` consistent with regular wallets by _not_ importing keys from the connected signer
- avoid going through `createTransaction` for external signers (otherwise the GUI breaks)
- create an `ExternalSignerScriptPubKeyMan` when importing a descriptor into an external signer wallet, instead of requiring an additional reload

This should have no noticeable effect on the default single sig use case described above.

Finally we add test coverage for spending from an imported hot key descriptor in an external signer wallet. The wallet signs with its own keys before involving the external signer.

pulls.title: wallet: harden the read-only BDB parser against crafted files
pulls.body:
The read-only BDB parser in migrate.cpp runs on any file passed to `migratewallet`
(RPC or GUI) or `bitcoin-wallet`. #34959 added checks for btree levels and overflow
lengths, which stop simple cycles, but a crafted file can still make the parser hang
or use a lot of memory:

- A btree page can be the child of more than one internal page. Its level still
  checks out, so it gets parsed again for every path that reaches it. On master an
  ~8 KB file built this way doesn't finish.
- An overflow page with no data doesn't count toward the length #34959 checks, so
  two such pages pointing at each other loop forever. Separately, any number of
  records can point at the same overflow chain, and each one reads and stores its
  own copy.
- All of a page's index entries can point at the same record, which then gets read
  and kept once per entry. A single 64 KB page can turn into ~500 MB this way. On
  master a 256 KB file took `migratewallet` from 54 MB to ~800 MB.

The first two are fixed by tracking visited pages (the approach from #34946): btree
pages in one set, and overflow pages in another that covers the whole tree. For the
third, a page is rejected once its records add up to more than the page size.

This shouldn't affect real wallets. In a valid btree every page has a single parent
and every overflow page belongs to a single record. Records on a page can't overlap
either, since the parser already rejects databases that allow duplicates.

Each fix comes with a test in db_tests.cpp that builds the bad file by hand, plus a
test that a page filled to the last byte still parses. `wallet_migration.py` passes
with v28.2.

The last commit adds two errors from #34959 to the `wallet_bdb_parser` fuzz target.
They were missing, so the target aborted on inputs that reach them. I ran into this
while feeding mutated copies of the test files through the target.

Supersedes #35992.

pulls.title: Interfaces: Expose UTXO Snapshot Loading and Add Progress Notifications
pulls.body:
# Add UTXO Snapshot Loading Interface and Progress Notifications

This PR implements a complete interface for loading UTXO snapshots through the GUI, including progress notifications to provide user feedback during the loading process.

---

## Changes

### Commit 1: interfaces: expose UTXO snapshot functionality (loading/activate) in node interface

- Added a new virtual method `snapshot` to the node interface for loading UTXO snapshots from a path.
- Added `snapshot.h` to `src/interfaces` defining the Snapshot interface; `activate()` returns `util::Result<const CBlockIndex*>` to   carry either the base block index on success or a descriptive error message on failure, matching the shape of `ChainstateManager::ActivateSnapshot()`.
- Added a `getMetadata` accessor so callers can read snapshot metadata populated during activation without re-parsing the file.
- Added `SnapshotImpl` in src/node/interfaces.cpp: opens the snapshot file, parses metadata, and forwards to `ChainstateManager::ActivateSnapshot()`, propagating any error as util::Error{...}.

This change enhances the user's ability to load UTXO snapshots through the GUI and/or RPC.

### Commit 2: `notifications: Implement snapshot load progress notifications`

- Added a new signal `SnapshotLoadProgress` for snapshot load progress in the UI interface.
- Updated the notifications interface to include a method for reporting snapshot loading progress.
- Enhanced the `ChainstateManager` to report progress during snapshot loading.
- Implemented the necessary handler in the kernel notifications to relay progress updates.

This change improves user feedback during the snapshot loading process.

### Commit 3: `rpc: refactor loadtxoutset to use snapshot interface`

- Updated the `loadtxoutset` RPC to call the new snapshot interface instead of directly working with chainstate internals. File opening, metadata parsing, and activation now all happen inside `interfaces::Snapshot::activate()` rather than being split between the RPC handler and the interface.
- Removed the redundant pre-parse block in the RPC handler; its file-open and metadata-parse work duplicated what activate() already performs.
- Collapsed the RPC error handling to a single `RPC_INTERNAL_ERROR` built from `util::ErrorString(activation_result).original`, using the `"Unable to load UTXO snapshot: %s. (%s)"` format established in #30267 / #30395.
- Read `coins_loaded` from `snapshot->getMetadata()` after `activate()` populates it.
- Updated `feature_assumeutxo.py` to assert on the unified error code for file-open and metadata-parse failures (message substrings unchanged).
Improves modularity by consolidating snapshot handling through the interface layer.
---

## Technical Details

The implementation includes:

- **UI Interface Enhancement**
  Added `SnapshotLoadProgress` signal to `CClientUIInterface` with corresponding signal declaration and implementation.

- **Node Interface**
  Added `loadSnapshot` virtual method to the node interface with implementation in `interfaces.cpp`.

- **Progress Notifications**
  Implemented `snapshotLoadProgress` method in `KernelNotifications` class to relay progress updates to the UI.

- **Base Interface**
  Added `snapshotLoadProgress` virtual method to the kernel notifications interface.

---

## Benefits

- **User Experience**
  Provides real-time feedback during UTXO snapshot loading operations.

- **GUI Integration**
  Enables loading UTXO snapshots directly through the Bitcoin Core GUI.

- **Progress Tracking**
  Users can monitor the progress of snapshot loading operations.

- **Consistent Interface**
  Follows the existing pattern for progress notifications in the codebase.

## Testing

- **Daemon** build and launch `bitcoind` then with `bitcoin-cli` load a snapshot using:
```bash
./bitcoin-cli -rpcclienttimeout=0 -signet loadtxoutset /path/to/utxo-snapsshot.dat
```
- **QT Widgets**: build and run [this](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/gui/pull/870) draft PR in legacy gui repo 
- **QML** version: for a modern look build and run [this](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/gui-qml/pull/488) PR in the newly updated gui-qml repo

pulls.title: node: batch block file pruning in a single pass over block index
pulls.body:
When starting a node with pruning enabled (e.g. `-prune=550`) on a node with full chain history or pruning many files at once, `FindFilesToPrune` and `FindFilesToPruneManual` previously called `PruneOneBlockFile` once per file.

Because `PruneOneBlockFile` iterated over the entire `m_block_index` for each file, this was an O(M * N) operation (M = files to prune, N = total blocks). When pruning a full chain (~5,770 files and ~972k blocks), this triggered ~5.6 billion iterations and froze the node running on a Pi 5 for ~10 minutes on startup while holding `cs_main`.

This PR replaces `PruneOneBlockFile` with `PruneBlockFiles(const std::set<int>&)`, which collects all candidate files and prunes them in a single O(M + N) pass over `m_block_index` using a compact dynamic bitfield (`std::vector<bool>`). Also skips entries without block or undo data to avoid unneeded checks and prevent file 0 pruning from dirtying header-only or already-pruned index entries. The new signature is analogous to `UnlinkPrunedFiles({file_number});`.

Benchmarked with ~972k blocks and 5,770 files to prune:
- x86_64 (i7-8665U @ 1.90 GHz): 75.1s -> 14.7ms (~5,100x speedup)
- ARM64 (Raspberry Pi 5): 606.0s -> 26.3ms (>3,500x speedup)

Both timings were taken with a datadir whose block index and block file info records came from a full chain, with the `blk*.dat` and `rev*.dat` files backfilled as 0-byte files. Pruning selection reads only the index and the file info, so empty files reproduce the startup cost without a full chain, and `UnlinkPrunedFiles` deletes them cheaply.

A case where this matters in practice is a pruned node restarting after a long outage. It downloads headers for the whole gap first, leaving many header-only entries behind, then has to prune a large backlog in a few flushes. The data-less skip avoids re-dirtying all of those entries, and the single pass bounds the work by the index size instead of files times index size.

Add unit test `blockmanager_prune_block_files_batch` to verify batch pruning, empty set no-ops, clean dirty-set behavior, and cleared block and undo metadata. Add a test for the `FindFilesToPruneManual` caller path, including a mixed valid and out-of-range file set. Update caller tests in `blockmanager_tests` and `rescan_tests`.

pulls.title: blocks: add resumable reobfuscation for existing block files
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Nodes that synced before v28 may store block and undo files effectively unobfuscated with a zero XOR key. There is no built-in way to obfuscate those existing files, rotate their key, or deliberately replace it with a zero key without resyncing.

**Fix:** Add `-reobfuscate-blocks[=<value>]` to rewrite existing `blk*.dat` and `rev*.dat` files before chainstate loading. With no value or `=1`, the option generates a random 8-byte key. A 16-character hexadecimal value selects an exact key, including all zeros to remove obfuscation, while malformed values fail during startup. If the selected key is already active, block and undo files are left unchanged.

Files are rewritten in fixed-size chunks, staged with a `.reobfuscated` suffix, committed before the originals are removed, and renamed to their original names after all rewrites finish. The target key is staged as `xor.dat.reobfuscated`, which is also used to resume an interrupted migration. Progress is reported in the log and through kernel notifications marked as resumable.

**Benchmark:** The migration is single-threaded and processes one file at a time.

| CPU | Storage | Block count | Size | Files | Time (min) | Blocks/min |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Apple M4 Max laptop | SSD | ~955k | ~854 GB | 11,232 | 10.18 | 93,804 |
| Intel Core i9 | SSD | ~909k | ~725 GB | 10,238 | 23.1 | 39,351 |
| Raspberry Pi 5 | SSD | ~914k | ~728 GB | 10,276 | 72.78 | 12,558 |
| Intel Core i7 | HDD | ~909k | ~720 GB | 10,156 | 208.7 | 4,356 |
| Raspberry Pi 4B | HDD | ~915k | ~730 GB | 10,304 | 1467 | 624 |
